Word and PowerPoint carry the text and leave the shaping to the application that opens them, so Arabic comes out right without this server carrying a text-shaping engine. A PDF has no such luxury: the glyphs and their order are fixed at the moment it is written, and no PDF library available to a Node service joins Arabic letters or reorders a bidirectional line. So the PDF is not written by a library at all — the pack is printed by a real browser on the server, the same one that renders it on screen. Arabic is therefore shaped by the same engine that has been doing it correctly for twenty years, and the document always matches the page, because it is the page.

Word and PowerPoint carry the text and leave the shaping to the application that opens them, so Arabic comes out right without this server carrying a text-shaping engine. Word and PowerPoint carry the text and leave the shaping to the application that opens them, so Arabic comes out right without this server carrying a text-shaping engine. A PDF has no such luxury: the glyphs and their order are fixed at the moment it is written, and no PDF library available to a Node service joins Arabic letters or reorders a bidirectional line. So the PDF is not written by a library at all — the pack is printed by a real browser on the server, the same one that renders it on screen. Arabic is therefore shaped by the same engine that has been doing it correctly for twenty years, and the document always matches the page, because it is the page.

Word and PowerPoint carry the text and leave the shaping to the application that opens them, so Arabic comes out right without this server carrying a text-shaping engine. A PDF has no such luxury: the glyphs and their order are fixed at the moment it is written, and no PDF library available to a Node service joins Arabic letters or reorders a bidirectional line. So the PDF is not written by a library at all — the pack is printed by a real browser on the server, the same one that renders it on screen. Arabic is therefore shaped by the same engine that has been doing it correctly for twenty years, and the document always matches the page, because it is the page.

Word and PowerPoint carry the text and leave the shaping to the application that opens them, so Arabic comes out right without this server carrying a text-shaping engine. A PDF has no such luxury: the glyphs and their order are fixed at the moment it is written, and no PDF library available to a Node service joins Arabic letters or reorders a bidirectional line. So the PDF is not written by a library at all — the pack is printed by a real browser on the server, the same one that renders it on screen. Arabic is therefore shaped by the same engine that has been doing it correctly for twenty years, and the document always matches the page, because it is the page.

Word and PowerPoint carry the text and leave the shaping to the application that opens them, so Arabic comes out right without this server carrying a text-shaping engine. A PDF has no such luxury: the glyphs and their order are fixed at the moment it is written, and no PDF library available to a Node service joins Arabic letters or reorders a bidirectional line. So the PDF is not written by a library at all — the pack is printed by a real browser on the server, the same one that renders it on screen. Arabic is therefore shaped by the same engine that has been doing it correctly for twenty years, and the document always matches the page, because it is the page.
